title: Looking spoils it
subtitle: The double-slit experiment as a circuit: why “peeking at the path” erases interference.

steps.title: One particle, two slits
body: In 1801, Thomas Young shone light through two slits and saw bright and dark stripes on a wall: interference, the signature of waves.

A century later, it turned out light arrives in packets (photons). In 1974, Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi in Bologna sent electrons one at a time through an equivalent setup; in 1989, Akira Tonomura and colleagues filmed the pattern building up. Each electron shows up as a tiny dot… but add up thousands, and the stripes appear.
Each electron, on its own, “interferes with itself”. Until someone tries to find out which slit it went through.

steps.title: The double slit becomes a circuit
body: Let's use a cleaner version: the Mach–Zehnder interferometer. A half-silvered mirror splits the photon into two paths; another half-silvered mirror joins them again.
In the circuit, each half-silvered mirror is an H. The upper path is 0, the lower path is 1. The measurement result tells you which detector the photon reached.

steps.title: No peeking
steps.body: Two half-silvered mirrors (H, H). Send photons, one at a time.
steps.after: All at detector 0! The two paths interfere: constructively at detector 0, destructively at 1. Just like the double-slit stripes.

steps.title: Now with a detector on the path
steps.body: A second qubit plays the role of a detector that records the path: a CNOT notes “went through the bottom” without pushing or slowing the photon.
steps.after: Look only at the first digit (the photon): now it's 0 and 1 half and half. The interference is gone. The detector didn't disturb the photon “by force” — it was enough for the path information to exist somewhere.

options.text: The detector gave the photon a “push”.
options.why: The CNOT doesn't touch the photon: it only changes the detector when the photon takes the bottom path. And yet the interference vanished.

options.text: The path information got recorded (entangled) in the detector, so the paths were no longer indistinguishable.
options.why: Right. Interference only happens between possibilities the universe can't tell apart. It's decoherence in miniature.

options.text: Detectors are classical and “break” quantum physics.
options.why: Here the detector is another qubit — everything stays quantum. What matters is the information, not the size of the detector.

steps.title: Erase the clue
steps.goal: The detector has already recorded the path. Use the free slot, before the last mirror, to erase that information and make the photon always reach detector 0 again.
hints: The CNOT is its own inverse.
Make the detector “un-record” the path with the same gate that recorded it.
steps.success: Information erased, interference restored! This is the idea behind quantum eraser experiments. On the sphere, the photon's arrow grew back.

steps.title: The most beautiful experiment
steps.text: In 2002, readers of Physics World voted the double slit with single electrons “the most beautiful experiment in physics”. Richard Feynman said it contains “the only mystery” of quantum mechanics.

takeaways: Single particles produce interference patterns, like waves.
Recording the path — anywhere — destroys the interference.
Erasing the path information can restore it: what counts is what the universe can tell apart.
